capitals.name: Azougui (Adrar)

correction.text: the 1126 shape plus the Hammadid part of the Oran-Tlemcen country, without the Saharan wing, valid 1119-1138: al-Andalus without the Ebro basin, Morocco, western Algeria and the Balearic Islands

correction.text: the 1139 shape plus the Oran-Tlemcen country and the southern Moroccan lands (Sous, Draa, Tafilalt with Sijilmasa) of the 1126 shape, held until 1144-1147

keyframe_review.note: Valid 1139-1143. Cliopatria's 421,000 km2 shape drops about 1.4 M km2 of the 1126 shape: the Saharan wing (4,003 cells, about 1.04 M km2), southern Morocco (1,552 cells, about 420,000 km2) and the Oran-Tlemcen country (173 cells; the rest of the 1126 shape is the same). The Saharan wing left in 1087 (ledger split). The Almohad page has Tlemcen captured 'in 1144', Oran in 1145, Fez in 1146 and Marrakesh in 1147, so the Oran-Tlemcen country is put back until then; southern Morocco (Sijilmasa taken 1054-55, the Sous and Draa with it) is put back too: no page records its loss before the fall of Marrakesh in 1147, and the Cliopatria shapes held it to 1138, so the 1139 drop is read as the shape's artefact, not a loss.

correction.text: the 1139 shape, southern Morocco and Oran without Tlemcen, without southwestern Iberia (Silves, Mertola, Beja, Evora) in the Muridun revolt

correction.text: the 1139 shape and southern Morocco, without Oran and Tenes (Almohads) and without the southwestern and eastern taifas of 1144-1145

region.text: the Saharan homeland (Cliopatria's 1056 shape without Aghmat and the Sous valley, Mauritania, Western Sahara, the Draa fringe) with Sijilmasa and Awdaghust, 'captured in 1054 or 1055'

ledger.note: 1054: the Almoravids take Sijilmasa and Awdaghust. 'Both cities were captured in 1054 or 1055' and the infobox gives 'Established: 1050s'; the movement began with the pilgrimage of Yahya ibn Ibrahim 'around 1040', and Abdullah ibn Yasin was expelled by the Gudala 'sometime in the 1040s'. The page names the cities, not a boundary, and does not say who held them. [fx-26, F051: the region was only two discs round Sijilmasa and Awdaghust (1,640 cells, 852 of them outside the 1056 shape: Hodh el Gharbi, Assaba, Kayes, Bechar, Meknes-Tafilalet) and left out the Saharan homeland, so the 1056 keyframe added 4,515 cells in one step. The page puts the movement's base in the Lamtuna heartland of the Adrar and the Sahara (stronghold Azuggi in the Adrar, the Lamtuna campaign to win over neighbouring tribes 'in the early 1050s', a battle in the Draa valley c. 1054) but gives no boundary; the homeland is taken as Cliopatria's 1056 shape less the lands the page dates later (Sous valley by 1056, Aghmat 1058). Town discs cut to 60 km.]

ledger.counterpart: Sous valley and Taroudant (rulers not named on the page)
ledger.note: By 1056: the Almoravids hold the Sous valley. 'By 1056, they had conquered Taroudant and the Sous Valley' (Almoravid page); the Draa valley battle is dated c. 1054 and Aghmat follows in 1058. The admin-1 Souss - Massa - Draa (Morocco) stands for the valley. Added by fx-26 (F051): the 1056 keyframe holds the Sous (271 cells) while the ledger gave it nowhere.

region.text: Aghmat, south of the later Marrakesh

ledger.counterpart: Aghmat (rulers not named on the page)
ledger.note: 1058: Aghmat falls. 'In 1058, they crossed the High Atlas and conquered Aghmat' (the capital until the founding of Marrakesh); the page does not name its rulers.
1058: the Almoravids reach the Barghawata. 'Abdullah ibn Yasin was killed in battle with them in 1058 or 1059.' The Barghawata dossier dates the first contact to 1058.
1060: the Barghawata fall. 'By 1060, however, they were conquered by Abu Bakr ibn Umar and were forced to convert to orthodox Islam.'
1060: the Almoravids hold the Barghawata country. The page's 'by 1060' makes 1060 a latest date; Cliopatria keeps the Barghawata to 1065 and adds the land to the Almoravid shape in 1066.

1070: Marrakesh founded as the new capital. 'Abu Bakr ibn Umar founded the new capital of Marrakesh'; the page gives 1070 as the common date, with sources from 1062 to 1078 (Yusuf page: 'Abu Bakr started the work on Marrakesh' in 1070). The seat moves from Aghmat.

region.text: Fez and Meknes, with Volubilis and the Gharb

ledger.counterpart: Fez (rulers not named on the page)
ledger.note: 1070: Fez falls. 'Some modern authors cite the date of the final conquest of Fez as 1069 (461 AH)'; Ronald Messier gives 18 March 1070; 'other historians date it to 1074 or 1075' (the Yusuf page has 1075). 1070 is the middle reading and inside Cliopatria's 1072 shape.

ledger.counterpart: Tangier and Oujda (rulers not named on the page)
ledger.note: 1079: Tangier and Oujda taken. The Yusuf page lists '1079: Captured Tangier and Oujda'; the Almoravid page does not mention Tangier and has Oujda taken in 1081, on the way to Tlemcen.

ledger.counterpart: Tlemcen (holder not named; the Tlemcen timeline lists the Hammadids)
ledger.note: 1080: Tlemcen taken. The Yusuf page has '1080: Captured Tlemcen'; the Almoravid page has Yusuf return 'with an army in 1081 that captured Oujda and then conquered Tlemcen'. The Tlemcen page's timeline lists the Hammadid Emirate to 1083 and the Almoravids from then; the previous holder is not named by the pages that date the conquest.
1081: Nekor destroyed. 'In 1080-1081, the Almoravid leader Yusuf ibn Tashfin destroyed the city for the fourth and last time.' The Rif emirate ends under the Almoravids.

1082: Algiers occupied. 'He pressed on and by 1082 he had captured Algiers. Algiers became their easternmost outpost.' The Yusuf page has 'Captured Algiers, Tenes, and Oran' in '1082-83'. The Hammadid shape keeps Algiers throughout and the Hammadid page has the Almohads taking Algiers in 1152, so the page conflict is recorded as an occupation of Hammadid land, not an annexation.

region.text: Oran and Tenes, with the part of the Hammadid outline in the Oran-Tlemcen country

ledger.note: 1082: Oran and Tenes taken, with the Hammadid country round them. The Yusuf page dates the capture of 'Algiers, Tenes, and Oran' to 1082-83; 1082 is the first year of the span. The land comes from the Hammadids: the Hammadid dossier records the loss of the Oran-Tlemcen country of its 1056 outline (about 18,700 km2, Tenes among it) to the Almoravids in the same year; the Almoravid page does not name the rulers, the Hammadid and Tlemcen pages do.

1083: Ceuta surrenders. 'The city finally surrendered in June-July 1083' (other sources August 1084); 'After the Almoravid capture of Ceuta (1083) on the southern shore of the Strait of Gibraltar'. Ends the Taifa of Ceuta.

region.text: the Saharan wing of the confederation: Mauritania (the Adrar and Tagant, Azuggi), the Western Sahara, the Malian fringe and the Algerian desert fringe of Cliopatria's shapes

ledger.counterpart: Southern Almoravids of the Adrar (Azuggi): the descendants of Abu Bakr ibn Umar and of his brother Yahya
ledger.note: 1087: Abu Bakr ibn Umar dies and the Saharan wing parts from the Moroccan empire. 'After the death of Abu Bakr (1087), the confederation of Berber tribes in the Sahara was divided between the descendants of Abu Bakr and his brother Yahya'; the town of Azuggi 'acted as the capital of the southern Almoravids under him and his successors', and the empire was 'divided into two distinct but co-dependent parts' (Almoravid page). The Abu Bakr page: he died 'in November of 1087', had left the northern dominions to Yusuf in 1072, and Sijilmasa minted 'coins in Abu Bakr's name' until his death. The year is the page's; the page draws no boundary and does not say the south left the empire that year, so the region is the researcher's reading (confidence 2): Mauritania, the Western Sahara, the Malian corner and the desert of south-western Algeria (Saoura, Tindouf, Bechar) that Cliopatria's shapes carry from 1056, about 1.04 M km2. Burkhalter, cited on the page, argues the southern Almoravids could have ruled the Sahara to the end of the 12th century.
1090: Granada surrenders. 'In September 1090, Ibn Tashfin forced Granada to surrender to him and sent Abdallah ibn Buluggin into exile in Aghmat.'
1091: Cordoba taken. 'In early 1091, the Almoravids took control of Cordoba and turned towards Seville.' Cordoba is read as part of the Seville taifa's holdings; the page does not name who held it.
1091: Almeria captured. 'In late 1091, the Almoravids captured Almeria.'
1091: Seville falls. 'In September 1091, al-Mu'tamid surrendered Seville to the Almoravids and was exiled to Aghmat.'
1092: Murcia seized. 'In late 1091 or January 1092, Ibn Aisha, one of Ibn Tashfin's sons, seized control of Murcia.'

region.text: the whole Taifa of Badajoz without the Lisbon and Santarem country, which comes in November 1094 from Alfonso VI

ledger.note: 1094: Badajoz taken. 'Meanwhile, also in 1094, the Almoravids seized control of the entire Taifa kingdom of Badajoz.' Lisbon and Santarem lie inside Cliopatria's Badajoz outline but were held by Alfonso VI since 1090 (Alfonso VI page), so they are a separate gain in November 1094.

November 1094: Lisbon, Sintra and Santarem pass from Alfonso VI to the Almoravids. 'As the price for this alliance [with the king of Badajoz, 1090], Alfonso VI had obtained Lisbon, Sintra and Santarem, but lost them in November 1094 when his son-in-law Raymond of Burgundy, responsible for defending these cities, was defeated by the Almoravid army that had taken Badajoz shortly before' (Alfonso VI page). The Almoravid page has Sir ibn Abu Bakr 'occupying Lisbon and Santarem' in 1111 without naming a previous holder; no page opened records a loss between 1094 and 1111, so the 1111 sentence is read as a re-occupation or consolidation and no second gain is drawn.

1102: Valencia occupied. After the Cid died on 10 July 1099 and his widow Jimena held it, 'The Almoravids occupied the city after them'; Mazdali's siege began in early spring 1102. The Yusuf page puts Mazdali's capture of Valencia in late 1100.
1103: the Hammadids contest Tlemcen. 'In 1103-1104 the Hammadids defeated the Almoravids and took control of Tlemcen.'
1104: peace with the Hammadids. 'Eventually, in 1104, they signed a peace treaty with the Hammadids.' Tlemcen is in Almoravid hands again when the Almohads take it in 1144; no page dates the return.

1104: the occupation of Algiers is taken to end with the peace treaty with the Hammadids; the Almoravid page is silent on Algiers after 1082 (bridging judgement). The Algiers page (read 2026-10-19) is silent on the end of the Almoravid occupation and lists 'the Almoravid Empire' at Algiers 1082-1151 in its timeline without explanation, while the Hammadid page has the Hammadids at Algiers until the Almohads in 1152; 1104 stays a bridge.

1110: Zaragoza taken, the last independent taifa. 'On 30 May, Ibn al-Hajj entered the city with little opposition, ending the last independent Taifa kingdom.' The Albarracin, Alpuente and Tortosa taifas end the same year in Cliopatria.

ledger.counterpart: Balearic Islands (last local ruler Mubashir al-Dawla)
ledger.note: 1115: the Balearic Islands taken. 'In that same year the Almoravids captured the Balearic Islands'; 'The Almoravids occupied Majorca without a fight after the death of the last local Muslim ruler, Mubashir al-Dawla.'
1118: Zaragoza lost. After a siege begun on 22 May, 'it surrendered on 18 December' to Alfonso I of Aragon.
1144: Tlemcen lost. 'This allowed them to defeat Tashfin decisively and capture Tlemcen in 1144.'

region.text: southwestern Iberia: Silves, Mertola, Beja and Evora (the Algarve and the lower Alentejo)

ledger.counterpart: Muridun of Ibn Qasi (Silves, Mertola, Beja, Evora)
ledger.note: 1144: southwestern Iberia lost to the Muridun. 'The Muridun staged a major revolt in southwestern Iberia in 1144 under the leadership of the Sufi mystic Ibn Qasi' (Almoravid page). The Taifa page dates the second taifas of Silves, Mertola, Beja and Evora to 1144 (Mertola passed to Badajoz in 1145), which gives the places; the Ibn Qasi page has his revolt creating a taifa 'in Silves'. The region (the Faro, Beja and Evora districts) is the researcher's reading of 'southwestern Iberia'.

region.text: Oran and Tenes, with the rest of the Oran-Tlemcen country

ledger.note: 1145: Oran lost. 'Tashfin fled to Oran, which the Almohads then attacked and captured, and he died in March 1145 while trying to escape.' The region adds the rest of the Oran-Tlemcen country (Tlemcen itself fell in 1144), which the page does not name: the researcher's reading, hence confidence 2.
1145: Badajoz becomes a second taifa. Taifa page: 'Badajoz: 1145-1150 (to Almohads)'. The province is the researcher's reading of the taifa's land.
1145: Niebla becomes a second taifa. Taifa page: 'Niebla: 1145-1150? (to Almohads)'. The province of Huelva is the researcher's reading.

1145: Almeria becomes a second taifa. Taifa page: 'Almeria: 1145-1147 (briefly to Castile and then to Almohads)'; the Alfonso VII page has Almeria 'occupied in October 1147' by his allied force and entering Almohad hands six years after the 1151 treaty. The province is the researcher's reading.

region.text: Valencia (the provinces of Valencia and Castellon)

ledger.note: 1145: Valencia becomes a second taifa. Taifa page: 'Valencia: 1145-1172 (to Almohads)'; the Yahya ibn Ghaniya page has him governing Murcia and Valencia from 1133 to 1145. The two provinces are the researcher's reading.

ledger.counterpart: second taifas of Malaga and Jaen (no Cliopatria row)
ledger.note: 1145: Malaga and Jaen become second taifas. Taifa page: 'Malaga: 1145-1153 (to Almohads)', 'Jaen: 1145-1159 (to Murcia); 1168 (to Almohads)'. The Yahya ibn Ghaniya page has him expelled from Jaen by Alfonso VII, undated. The same list dates Granada to 1145, but the Banu Ghaniya page calls Granada 'the last outpost of Almoravid rule' where Yahya died in 1148 or 1149, so Granada is kept (disagreement noted).
1146: Fez lost. Fez fell 'in 1146 after a nine-month siege'.

region.text: Morocco: Marrakesh and the rest of the 1139 shape outside Iberia and the Balearic Islands

ledger.note: 1147: Marrakesh falls and the dynasty with it. 'They finally captured Marrakesh in 1147, after an eleven-month siege.' The Almoravid page: 'The conquest of Marrakesh by the Almohads in 1147 marked the fall of the dynasty.'

1147: the dynasty of Yusuf ibn Tashfin ends at Marrakesh; its Balearic branch, the Banu Ghaniya, 'a branch of the Almoravids', continues. The page gives no month or year for the break and says only that Muhammad 'became independent after Yahya's death in late 1148 or early 1149'. One state, one colour, as Cliopatria draws it to 1205.

region.text: southern Morocco: the Sous, the Draa and the Tafilalt with Sijilmasa

ledger.note: 1147: southern Morocco goes with the dynasty. 'The conquest of Marrakesh by the Almohads in 1147 marked the fall of the dynasty.' No page opened dates the Sous, the Draa or Sijilmasa in the 1140s (the Abd al-Mu'min page has Sijilmasa and other cities overthrowing their Almohad governors, undated, and the Sous at the centre of that rebellion), so the year is a bridging judgement from the fall of the capital.

region.text: Algeciras and Tarifa (the province of Cadiz)

ledger.note: 1147: Algeciras and Tarifa fall to the Almohads. The Abd al-Mu'min page has his army 'captured Algeciras and Tarifa before moving west to Niebla, Badajoz, and the Algarve'; the Yahya ibn Ghaniya page has the Almohads landing in al-Andalus in 1146. The province is the researcher's reading.

region.text: Murcia (the provinces of Murcia and Alicante)

ledger.note: 1147: Murcia becomes a second taifa. Taifa page: 'Murcia: 1147-1172 (to Almohads)'. The two provinces are the researcher's reading.

15 March 1147: Santarem falls to Afonso I of Portugal. 'The period of Arabic domination was finished in 1147 by the first King of Portugal, Afonso Henriques', who 'conquered the city on March 15' after men climbed the walls at night (Santarem page; the Siege of Lisbon page has the same date without the year, the Afonso I page a footnote reading 15 May).

25 October 1147: Lisbon falls to Afonso I and the crusaders. The siege ran '1 July - 25 October 1147'; the rulers 'agreed to surrender' on 21 or 24 October and the city 'was entered by the Christian conquerors, on 25 October'; the page's infobox names the Almoravid dynasty as the defender and the Almoravid page has 'Lisbon was conquered by the Portuguese in 1147'. The 'surrounding territories' the page says were 'soon captured' are not named, so only the Lisbon circle is drawn here; the rest of the Portuguese part of the shape goes in the 1149 bridge.

1148: Seville falls to the Almohads. 'The city was captured in 1148 with local support' (Abd al-Mu'min page); the Almohad page's infobox lists Seville as the Almohad capital in al-Andalus from 1147. The province is the researcher's reading.

1149: Cordoba falls to the Almohads. 'They took control of Cordoba in 1149' (Abd al-Mu'min page); the Yahya ibn Ghaniya page has him defending it unsuccessfully against Alfonso VII in 1146. The province is the researcher's reading.

region.text: the rest of the Iberian shape outside Granada: the Tagus and Guadiana marches and the La Mancha and Ebro fringe that Cliopatria draws

ledger.counterpart: Castile, Aragon, Portugal and the Almohads (not apportioned on the pages opened)
ledger.note: 1149: the last Almoravid land outside Granada is bridged out. The Abd al-Mu'min page has the Almoravids 'confined to Granada' before the defeat of 1155 and the Banu Ghaniya page calls Granada 'the last outpost of Almoravid rule' where Yahya died in late 1148 or early 1149; no page opened says who took Ciudad Real (77 cells), Albacete (59), Caceres (49), Cuenca (35), Teruel (35), Portalegre (22), Toledo (18), Setubal (15), Tarragona (13), Lerida (8) and the small parts of Santarem, Zaragoza, Huesca, Leiria and Lisboa outside the other events, which Cliopatria's 1139 shape draws (350 cells, about 88,000 km2) although most was Castilian or Aragonese ground; the shape has this land from 1094 with no gain event. The year is the researcher's bridge.

region.text: Granada, the last Almoravid outpost on the Iberian mainland

ledger.note: 1155: the last mainland remnant falls. 'The Almoravids in Granada were defeated in 1155' (Abd al-Mu'min page, which has them 'confined to Granada'); the Almoravid page: 'Also in 1155, the remaining Almoravids were forced to retreat to the Balearic Islands and later Ifriqiya.' The Banu Ghaniya page has Yahya ibn Ghaniya, 'the last outpost of Almoravid rule' at Granada, persuading its governor to surrender to the Almohads, undated, and dying there in late 1148 or early 1149; the 1155 year of the other two pages is followed. The province is the researcher's reading of the city's land.

region.text: Bougie, Constantine, Algiers and most of Tunisia

ledger.note: 1184: the Banu Ghaniya, claiming to be 'heir of the Almoravids' under the Abbasid caliph, invade the Almohad east. They 'undertook military campaigns against the Almohads in North Africa from November 1184' and made 'a determined attempt to reconquer the Maghreb (and in particular Ifriqiya), taking Bougie, Constantine and Algiers', and 'most of modern Tunisia from about 1180 onwards'. The pages give no boundary; the cities and Tunisia are named. Region check: the Banu Ghaniya page names only 'Bougie, Constantine and Algiers' as cities but also says they conquered 'most of modern Tunisia' from about 1180, which the Tunisia part of the region follows; it names no towns or years for Yahya ibn Ishaq after 1188 (he 'remained active in Ifriqiya until driven out in 1226').

region.text: the Balearic Islands, retaken by the Almohads while Ali ibn Ishaq was in the eastern Maghreb

ledger.note: 1185: the Almohads retake the Balearic Islands. 'In his absence [Ali ibn Ishaq was campaigning in the eastern Maghreb], the Almohads retook the islands in 1185.' The rulers table lists Muhammad ibn Ishaq (second reign) from 1185 and Tashfin ibn Ishaq to 1187 without saying where they ruled.

region.text: the Balearic Islands, recaptured by Abdallah ibn Ishaq

ledger.note: By 1187: Abdallah ibn Ishaq recaptures the Balearic Islands from the Almohads ('Recaptured the islands from the Almohads by 1187'); the page gives no date or method, so the year is the page's latest and the keyframe starts there.

region.text: Bougie, Constantine, Algiers and most of Tunisia

ledger.note: 1188: the Almohads reclaim Ifriqiya. 'Yaqub al-Mansur reconquered Ifriqiya in 1187-1188.' The Banu Ghaniya page has their campaigns running to 1237/1238 in raids. Region check: the Banu Ghaniya page names only 'Bougie, Constantine and Algiers' as cities but also says they conquered 'most of modern Tunisia' from about 1180, which the Tunisia part of the region follows; it names no towns or years for Yahya ibn Ishaq after 1188 (he 'remained active in Ifriqiya until driven out in 1226').

1203: the Almohads take the Balearic Islands. Abdallah ibn Ishaq was 'defeated and executed by the Almohads in 1203, who installed their own governors on the islands after this'; 'the Banu Ghaniya continued to govern the Balearic Islands as independent emirs until about 1203'.

wars.name: Almoravid conquest of the Barghawata
wars.outcome: Almoravid victory: 'By 1060, however, they were conquered by Abu Bakr ibn Umar and were forced to convert to orthodox Islam'; Abdullah ibn Yasin was killed in the fighting in 1058 or 1059.

wars.name: Almoravid conquest of the northern Maghreb

zones.text: Fez, Tangier, Oujda, Tlemcen, Nekor, Algiers, Oran and Ceuta, taken one by one

wars.outcome: Yusuf ibn Tashfin's conquests: Fez 1070 (or 1069/1074/75), Tangier and Oujda 1079, Tlemcen 1080/81, Nekor 1080-81, Algiers, Tenes and Oran 1082-83, Ceuta 1083. Algiers is held only as an outpost.
wars.note: The Almoravid page and the Yusuf page differ by one to six years on Fez, Tlemcen and Ceuta; both are cited in the ledger notes.

wars.name: Battle of Sagrajas (az-Zallaqah)
wars.outcome: Almoravid victory on 23 October 1086: 'Alfonso was soundly defeated'. No land changes hands at once; the crossing leads to the deposition of the taifa kings from 1090.

wars.name: Almoravid conquest of the taifas
wars.outcome: Granada Sept 1090, Cordoba and Seville 1091, Almeria late 1091, Murcia 1092, Badajoz 1094, Valencia 1102, Zaragoza 30 May 1110 ('ending the last independent Taifa kingdom').

wars.name: Hammadid-Almoravid war over Tlemcen
wars.outcome: The Hammadid page: 'In 1103-1104 the Hammadids defeated the Almoravids and took control of Tlemcen'; the Almoravid page: 'in 1104, they signed a peace treaty with the Hammadids'.
wars.note: The pages disagree on who ended up with Tlemcen; the Almohads take it from the Almoravids in 1144.

wars.name: Siege of Zaragoza (1118)
wars.outcome: Alfonso I of Aragon took Zaragoza: the siege 'began on 22 May and, after no significant reinforcements arrived, it surrendered on 18 December'.

wars.name: Battle of Cutanda
wars.outcome: 'A serious defeat at the Battle of Cutanda in 1120' for the Almoravids; no zone named on the page.

wars.name: Battle of Fraga
wars.outcome: 'The most significant was the Battle of Fraga in 1134': listed among the setbacks of the Almoravids' decline; no territorial result on the page.
wars.note: The winner's side was read from the page's list of Almoravid setbacks; treated as a battle with no territorial result.

wars.name: Almohad conquest of the Almoravids

zones.text: Tlemcen, Oran, Fez and Marrakesh, lost in that order

wars.outcome: Ibn Tumart's base at Tinmel 'around 1124'; the Almoravids crush the Almohads at Marrakesh in April or May 1130; Tlemcen 1144, Oran 1145, Fez 1146, Marrakesh 1147 after an eleven-month siege.

wars.name: Banu Ghaniya campaigns in Ifriqiya
wars.outcome: The Banu Ghaniya took Bougie, Constantine and Algiers and much of Tunisia; 'Yaqub al-Mansur reconquered Ifriqiya in 1187-1188'; raids continue to 1237/38.

wars.name: Siege of Lisbon (1147)
wars.outcome: Portuguese-crusader victory: Santarem taken on 15 March 1147 and Lisbon on 25 October 1147 after a siege begun on 1 July; both cities leave the Almoravids.
wars.note: The Siege of Lisbon page names the Almoravid dynasty as the defending side; the Santarem date comes from the Santarem page.

wars.name: Almohad conquest of Almoravid al-Andalus

zones.text: southwestern Iberia, Algeciras and Tarifa, Seville, Cordoba and Granada

wars.outcome: The Muridun revolt of 1144 and the second taifas of 1144-1147 end Almoravid rule in most of the peninsula; the Almohads take Algeciras and Tarifa (1147), Seville (1148), Cordoba (1149) and defeat the Almoravids in Granada in 1155, after which the remnant withdraws to the Balearic Islands and Ifriqiya.
wars.note: Alfonso VII occupies Almeria in October 1147 (Alfonso VII page); the Almohad page says the Almohads wrested Iberia from the Almoravids 'between 1146 and 1173', which describes the second taifas as well.

certainty.note: No treaty or survey lines exist for the whole life: the Saharan homeland is nomad country with no boundary, the Andalusian frontier with the Christian kingdoms moves with campaigns (Zaragoza lost 1118), and the sources name cities, not frontiers. The Strait coast (Ceuta) and the Balearic Islands are the only clear edges.

sources.title: Emirate of Nekor

sources.title: Tlemcen

sources.title: Takrur

sources.title: Abu Bakr ibn Umar
sources.note: Abu Bakr's return to the Sahara, the northern dominions left to Yusuf in 1072, his death in November 1087 and the coins of Sijilmasa in his name.

sources.title: Siege of Lisbon
sources.note: The siege of Lisbon, 1 July to 25 October 1147; the Almoravid dynasty as the defender.

sources.title: Santarem, Portugal

sources.title: Abd al-Mu'min

sources.title: Alfonso VI of Leon and Castile

sources.title: Alfonso VII of Leon and Castile

sources.title: Yahya ibn Ghaniya
sources.note: Yahya defending Cordoba in 1146, the Almohad landing, his death in Granada in 1148.

sources.title: Ibn Qasi
sources.note: The Muridun revolt creating a taifa in Silves; Ibn Qasi's death in 1151.

sources.title: Algiers
sources.note: Silent on the end of the Almoravid occupation of Algiers; timeline lists the Almoravid Empire 1082-1151.

sources.title: Afonso I of Portugal
sources.note: Santarem and Lisbon seized in 1147; a footnote reads 15 May 1147 for Santarem against 15 March on the Santarem page (thin: no Almoravid mention).

sources.title: Taifa of Badajoz
sources.note: Silent on Lisbon and Santarem in 1093-1094; gives only the Almoravid occupation of Badajoz in 1094 (thin for this purpose).

notes: Judgement calls. (1) Start 1054, not Cliopatria's 1056: the page puts the first captures (Sijilmasa, Awdaghust) in '1054 or 1055' and the infobox says '1050s'. (2) End 1203, not 1147: the Almoravid page ends the dynasty with the fall of Marrakesh in 1147, but the Banu Ghaniya of the Balearic Islands are 'a branch of the Almoravids' (Banu Ghaniya page), took the title 'heir of the Almoravids' from the Abbasid caliph, and Cliopatria draws them in this row to 1205; they are kept in one dossier (rule 2) with a rename event in 1147. A different reading would split them as a separate dossier 'Banu Ghaniya' for 1148-1203; the reviewer may prefer that. (3) Cliopatria's 1.4-1.9 M km2 shapes include about 1.04 M km2 of Saharan wing (about 755,000 km2 of Mauritania, the Western Sahara, 18,000 km2 in Mali and 161,000 km2 of Algerian desert); the pages bound none of it, so it stays soft. After the review it is drawn to 1086 and leaves in 1087 as a split to 'the southern Almoravids of the Adrar' (Almoravid page: after Abu Bakr's death in 1087 the Saharan confederation 'was divided' between his descendants and Yahya's, the south ruling from Azuggi), which brings the 1111 shape to about 0.89 M km2 against the infobox's 1,000,000 km2 for 1120. Southern Morocco (Sous, Draa, Tafilalt with Sijilmasa), which Cliopatria's 1139 shape drops, is kept to 1147 (no page records an earlier loss) and lost with the fall of Marrakesh at confidence 1. Awdaghust is inside the shape; the Ghana Empire (Cliopatria 793-1201) does not overlap it; Takrur was an ally. The Ghana conquest 'sometime around 1076-77' is Arab tradition, disputed by later scholars (Almoravid page) and is not drawn. (4) Pages disagree: Fez 1069 / 1070 / 1074-75 (Almoravid page) or 1075 (Yusuf page); Tlemcen 1080 (Yusuf) or 1081 (Almoravid); Ceuta June-July 1083 or August 1084; Valencia 1102 (Almoravid) or late 1100 (Yusuf); the Tlemcen timeline lists the Hammadids until 1083 while the Hammadid page has them taking Tlemcen only in 1103-04. (5) Algiers: two pages say the Almoravids took it in 1082, but the Hammadid shape keeps it and the Hammadid page has the Almohads taking it in 1152; recorded as an occupation to 1104 at low confidence. (6) Al-Andalus 1144-1155 (rebuilt after the review): the first draft kept the whole Iberian part of the 1139 shape Almoravid to 1155, four years past Cliopatria's own Iberian end (1151). Now: southwestern Iberia to the Muridun (1144, Almoravid page), the second taifas of Badajoz, Niebla, Almeria, Valencia, Malaga and Jaen (1145) and Murcia (1147) from the Taifa page's list, Santarem (15 March 1147) and Lisbon (25 October 1147) to Portugal, Algeciras and Tarifa (1147), Seville (1148) and Cordoba (1149) to the Almohads (Abd al-Mu'min page), and Granada, 'the last outpost of Almoravid rule', defeated in 1155. Lisbon, Sintra and Santarem are a November 1094 gain from Alfonso VI (Alfonso VI page), and the 1111 'occupying Lisbon and Santarem' sentence of the Almoravid page is read as a re-occupation. Weak points: the provinces used for the taifas are the researcher's reading; the Taifa page dates Granada to 1145 (kept Almoravid on the Banu Ghaniya and Abd al-Mu'min pages); the La Mancha, Extremadura and Ebro fringe of Cliopatria's shape (350 cells) has no gain event and is bridged out in 1149 at confidence 1; the Balearic Islands are Almohad in 1185-1186 with no keyframe those years. Not drawn for lack of a dated page: the Banu Ghaniya raids in Ifriqiya after 1188 to 1237/38 (Yahya ibn Ishaq, 'driven out in 1226' on the Banu Ghaniya page). Gazetteer names that do not resolve and are real: Aghmat and Tenes are used as coordinate radii (31.36N 7.85W; 36.51N 1.31E). Counterparts without a dossier: Banu Ghaniya revival (1184-1237) for the Maghreb group; Muridun of Ibn Qasi; the southern Almoravids of the Adrar (1087-c.1200); the second taifas of Malaga and Jaen; Alfonso VI's realm is taken as kingdom-of-leon. Hammadid mirror: the Hammadid dossier's 1082 loss of the Oranais is now matched by the 1082 gain here (Hammadid outline within the Oranais, with Oran and Tenes). Rulers not listed: the pages opened give Yusuf ibn Tashfin 1061-1106 only, no list. Method note: every page was read through WebFetch, which returns a model-made extraction; phrases in quotation marks are the extraction's wording of the page and may differ in small ways from the live text, while the years and months are the ones it reported.
